from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('pages', len(r.pages))
print('metadata',r.metadata)
parts=[]
for n,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 t=p.extract_text()
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {n} =====\\n\\n'+t)
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{n:02}.txt').write_text(t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts)[:30000])
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical question for NLP-assisted qualitative research: how collaboration settings affect the outputs of interactive coding tools.

Evaluating three different system families on two contrasting corpora offers useful comparative evidence. Shared initializations within systems reduce one source of experimental variation, and separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness is conceptually helpful.

The manual evaluation of 2,400 document-theme pairs, with two annotators and adjudication, adds substantive evidence beyond embedding-based metrics. Reporting agreement separately for each corpus makes annotation uncertainty visible.
The manuscript is generally clear and supplies extensive appendices containing prompts, system operations, final theme lists, and corpus statistics, alongside a repository link.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. Section 4 compares three-person synchronous groups with individual coders, without reporting consolidation of the asynchronous code-books, despite including consolidation in the introductory definition. Group size, effort, and collaboration timing are therefore entangled. Reused participants always complete asynchronous work first, introducing possible practice effects. The evidence supports a narrower comparison of joint and individual coding under these protocols.

The statistical evidence for collaboration effects is insufficiently justified. Each system/dataset has only two synchronous and three asynchronous code-books, yielding just one synchronous code-book pair for consistency. Tables 1–2 use unpaired t-tests without specifying the observations or accounting for themes nested within code-books, overlapping comparisons, and repeated participants. Treating themes or document pairs as independent experimental replicates would constitute pseudoreplication. Numerous tests, 'near significant' results, and some very small differences further weaken the claims. Reanalysis must respect the experimental units and distinguish descriptive differences from supported population effects.

Correctness is not adequately defined for reproduction. Figure 4 reports F1, but Section 5.3 describes judging sampled document-theme assignments without explaining how false negatives or recall are obtained. Aggregation across themes, code-books, and quartiles is also unspecified, and the figure provides no uncertainty estimates. The scoring formula, annotation instructions, sampling weights, and treatment of unassigned documents are needed to interpret the reported system rankings.

The proposed quality metrics need stronger construct validation. Maximum-similarity matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to theme granularity, which varies substantially across sessions (Table 17). Selecting the closest 25% of documents using embedding geometry mechanically favors cohesion under related metrics. Semantic compactness also need not imply an analytically useful theme. Human assessment of code-book quality or sensitivity analyses are needed before these proxies support claims of deeper analysis and clearer themes.

Participant and code-book provenance is unclear. As written, the design requires 36 synchronous participant slots, yet only 33 researchers are reported and repeat participants supposedly attend at most one synchronous experiment. Tables 15–16 also contain identical Climate theme sets for the relational and LLM conditions. Clarifying participant allocation and whether code-books were reused is necessary to establish the number of independent experiments and reproduce the comparison.

Several conclusions exceed the design's explanatory power. Two corpora that differ simultaneously in domain, size, length, and semantic structure cannot establish that particular dataset characteristics independently cause the observed effects. Likewise, differences among three bundled systems do not isolate the benefit of richer intervention mechanisms. These are useful hypotheses, but the recommendations require narrower wording. The design, statistical, and scoring ambiguities affect the central contribution and prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.
